title: 10 Bizarre Medical Treatments
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant tour ten bizarre medical treatments from history, based on a HowStuffWorks article. Covered: Botox as a cosmetic oddity; tobacco enemas for drowning victims and the Royal Humane Society; mercury as an elixir and treatment, including China's first emperor Qin Shi Huang and syphilis treatments; the whirling chair for mental illness; radium-laced products such as radium water, bread, toothpaste and the Radithor tincture that killed Eben Byers; urine therapy; the pelvic massage for "hysteria" and the early vibrator; leeches and bloodletting, including George Washington's death and the FDA-approved medical leech; cocaine and opium in nineteenth-century over-the-counter medicines; trepanation, including Bart Huges and Amanda Feilding; and corpse medicine and mummy consumption. The episode ends with listener mail about pronouncing "the" in singing and a plug for a band's charity fundraiser.

segments.title: Opening banter and Botox
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about Botox injections, the film Dead Calm, and hyperhidrosis, then frame the episode around bizarre historical treatments drawn from a HowStuffWorks article. They also plug Sawbones.

segments.title: Tobacco enemas and drowning resuscitation
segments.summary: Tobacco smoke enemas were used to revive drowning victims, with a legend about a French man reviving his wife. Equipment was placed along rivers, and the Royal Humane Society was formed in 1774 and offered rewards. Dr Richard Mead is mentioned, and the practice was later abandoned.

segments.title: Mercury as an immortality elixir and treatment
segments.summary: Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, reportedly took mercury to become immortal and died before forty; his tomb is surrounded by liquid mercury. Mercury was later used to treat syphilis, with harmful effects. Cinnabar was used in China for two thousand years. The hosts discuss the claim about Jeremy Piven and mercury poisoning.

segments.title: The whirling chair
segments.summary: A mid-nineteenth-century device for mentally ill patients that spun a seated patient until they passed out, supposedly to shuffle brain contents and cure schizophrenia. Little information survives about it.

segments.title: Radium-laced products
segments.summary: Late nineteenth and early twentieth century products contained radium, including radium water, bread, chocolate, toothpaste, cosmetics, and a toy radium scope. Radium was promoted after hot springs were found to contain radon. The tincture Radithor was linked to the death of Eben Byers from radiation poisoning. Radium paint workers at US Radium Corporation were harmed, and radioactive bougies were used.

segments.title: Urine therapy
segments.summary: Urine therapy, or drinking one's own urine or injecting it, is described as based on the idea that urine reflects the blood's toxin level. The hosts say there is no scientific evidence it fights cancer, though people have survived by drinking urine, and it worsens jellyfish stings.

segments.title: Pelvic massage for hysteria and the early vibrator
segments.summary: Doctors treated women diagnosed with hysteria or wandering womb with pelvic massage to bring on 'hysterical paroxysm.' Physicians sought substitutes, and a vibrator was introduced in the late nineteenth century, sold through Sears and Roebuck, before being removed from medical use and appearing in erotic films in the 1920s.

segments.title: Leeches and bloodletting
segments.summary: Bloodletting by barber surgeons and leeches was used for thousands of years under humoral medicine. George Washington's doctors reportedly bled him heavily before his death. Medical leeches are still used today and are FDA approved; leech saliva contains hirudin, an anticoagulant with other useful properties.

segments.title: Cocaine and opium in patent medicines
segments.summary: Cocaine and opium were common in over-the-counter nineteenth-century medicines, including Coca-Cola, cocaine toothache drops, throat lozenges, cocaine wine (Vin Mariani), and opium-based products. Strong drugs were eventually restricted to prescriptions.

segments.title: Trepanation
segments.summary: Trepanation, or drilling holes in the skull, dates back thousands of years. The hosts discuss Bart Huges's theory about blood flow and Amanda Feilding, who drilled a hole in her own head in the 1970s and reported calmer dreams, while acknowledging a possible placebo effect.

segments.title: Corpse medicine and mummy consumption
segments.summary: Corpse medicine, or cannibalism for healing, included eating mummy powder, drinking gladiator blood for epilepsy, and rubbing human fat on the body. Mummy brown pigment was made from mummies until artists learned its origin.

segments.title: Listener mail: pronouncing 'the' in singing
segments.summary: A listener explains vocal-music rules for pronouncing 'the' before consonants and vowels and thanks a former vocal teacher. A plug for a band's fundraiser for Songs for Kids is also included, along with the show's contact info.
